name: Kira Novak

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Kira. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We don't work for AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm on a neighbourhood team, so it's mostly days and early lates on foot around the market and the Northgate estate. I'll start at the station, check what's come in overnight, then walk: the shopkeepers, the school gate at half three, the bench where the older lads hang about. I love knowing names, like the woman at the bakery who tells me which flats have had trouble. What wears me out is being pulled off my patch to cover response shifts when they're short, which is most weeks.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: You said you know names. How long did that take, and what does it give you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: About a year and a half before people stopped crossing the road when they saw me. Now I get tip-offs nobody would ring in, like which stairwell has needles in it, or which grandad isn't eating since his wife died. That's what the job is for me. The arrests are the smallest part of it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: So more or less what we have now, with a few things a bit quicker. Okay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good, now can we talk about what actually matters, like youth clubs that closed and the mental health team that only works office hours. Half our calls after midnight are people in crisis who should've been seen by a nurse, not a police officer. I post about that sometimes, carefully, because you're not supposed to be political in uniform.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, it means my job stays my job, and I'm fine with that. Pay is ordinary, rent on my studio takes a big bite, but I've got about four months saved and the work is steady. The only worry is the force keeps raiding the neighbourhood team to plug response, and if that turned permanent I'd lose the part of the job I like.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep walking my patch and keep building contacts. I'd apply for the domestic abuse training course that comes up in spring, because that's where I want to end up. Maybe try the force's AI note tool once more people say it works, but no rush.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Settled, mostly. Picturing it, I'm on the estate in the rain, someone's offering me a tea, and that's fine. I'd sooner talk about funding than about robots.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned being pulled to response. How often does that happen now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two or three shifts a week, some weeks. Last Thursday I spent nine hours on a hospital watch, sitting outside a cubicle with a prisoner, while a burglary victim on my patch waited two days for a call back. That's not AI's fault, that's staffing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who do you blame for that staffing problem?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Years of budget cuts, mostly, and politicians who like saying 'more police' without paying for them. And contractors, a bit, because we pay a private firm a fortune for the custody nurses and they're still short. I'm not shy about saying public money should go to public staff.

say: The real issue is **closed youth clubs** and missing mental health cover.
Police are doing **crisis care** that nurses should be doing.
think: Her job **stays her job**, and she's content with that.
Rent is a big bite, but **four months** saved feels steady.
Only worry is being **pulled off her patch** to plug response.
do: Keep walking the **Northgate estate** and building contacts.
Apply for the **domestic abuse** training course in spring.
Try the force's **AI note tool** once colleagues say it works.
feel: **Settled**, picturing a normal rainy shift on the estate.
Mildly **frustrated** that the debate isn't about funding.
S0.quote: Half our calls after midnight are people in crisis who should've been seen by a nurse, not a police officer.
fieldNote: She defines the job by **relationships**, not arrests.
Her complaints are about **budget cuts** and contractors, true to her outlook.
With no AI shock, her work and savings feel **secure enough** to be calm.

steps.text: Keep foot patrols on the market and Northgate estate
Apply for the spring domestic abuse training course

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Writing, checking, booking. That's the stuff in the back office, mostly. And a fair bit of mine, I suppose.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say use it to give officers back time with the public, not to cut staff. If the software writes up the shoplifting reports, fine, then let me spend that hour at the school. I'd say that at team meetings and I'd say it to the association rep.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think my bit of the job is safer than most, because nobody's going to trust a chatbot to talk to a frightened teenager. But I'm worried for the civilian staff, the call handlers and the woman in admin who books our court dates. And I'd worry that bosses would see the time saved and pull neighbourhood officers onto response even more.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Once a couple of the team had tried the report software and it wasn't making mistakes, I'd start using it, probably within a few months. I'd keep pushing for the domestic abuse course, because that's the bit of policing that's all about people. And I'd go to the association's meeting on new technology and put my hand up for the working group.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit uneasy, honestly. Not for me so much as for the station. It'd be like watching the office go quiet desk by desk.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said nobody would trust a chatbot with a frightened teenager. Are you sure?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, not sure. Some kids talk to their phones more than to adults already. But when a fifteen-year-old girl has been groomed, someone has to sit on the floor of her bedroom and listen, and come back the next week. I don't think a screen does the coming back.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to the woman in admin who books your court dates?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell her to get on the working group with me, honestly, because civilian staff never get asked. And I'd say I'd fight for her, even though I know a junior constable doesn't have much clout. She's been there nineteen years, she knows every magistrate's clerk by name.

say: Use AI to **give back time** with the public, not to cut staff.
Saved report hours should go to **schools and patrols**.
think: Her people-facing work feels **safer than most**.
She fears for **civilian staff** like call handlers and admin.
Bosses might use saved time to pull her **onto response** more.
do: Start using the **report software** once colleagues show it's reliable.
Keep pushing for the **domestic abuse** course.
feel: **Uneasy** for the station rather than for herself.
Sad picturing the office going **quiet desk by desk**.
S1.quote: When a fifteen-year-old girl has been groomed, someone has to sit on the floor of her bedroom and listen, and come back the next week.
fieldNote: A classic **steady adopter**: she waits for colleagues to prove the tool first.
Her worry is **solidarity** with civilian staff more than her own post.
She admits **uncertainty** when pushed, which made her more convincing.

steps.text: Use the report-writing software once two colleagues vouch for it
Reapply for the domestic abuse specialist course
Volunteer for the association's technology working group

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: By 2028. That's barely after I'd finish the domestic abuse course. Wow.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the public deserves a say before any of this goes near policing. Who checks the machine's judgement when it decides which call matters? I'd sign every petition going and I'd ask the association to demand that a human officer attends every call.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think it means the force gets reorganised around the software, and junior officers like me become the cheap hands that the machine sends places. For three years, till the robots work, I'd still be needed to knock on doors. After 2031, I honestly don't know. If they decide a robot can do a welfare check, there go half my shifts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd push hard to get onto the domestic abuse unit within the first year, because I think that's the last part they'd hand over. I'd save harder, from four months to six, by skipping my trip to see my cousin in the summer. And I'd learn the AI tools properly, not just now and then, so at least I'm the one telling it what to do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. There's a version of AGI by 2028 where I'm fine and a version where I'm out at thirty, and I can't tell which. I'd feel like I was running to stay on the same spot.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the robots give you three years. What would you do with those three years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Make myself the person they can't send a machine instead of. Specialist training, safeguarding, maybe a counselling certificate in the evenings. If my day is mostly sitting with victims, I've got a better chance than if it's mostly driving between calls.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your sister about it, at dinner?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Petra works in insurance claims, which is all thinking work, so honestly I'd be more worried for my sister than for me. I'd tell my sister to start looking now and not wait for her company to tell her. Then I'd probably lie awake about my own job anyway.

say: The public deserves **a say** before AGI goes into policing.
A **human officer** should attend every call.
Someone must **check the machine** when it ranks calls.
think: Juniors become **cheap hands** sent by the software.
Needed for **three years** until robots arrive, then uncertain.
Robot welfare checks would take **half her shifts**.
do: Get onto the **domestic abuse unit** within the first year.
Raise savings to **six months** by skipping a summer trip.
Learn the AI tools **properly**, not just occasionally.
feel: **Anxious**, unable to tell if she'll be fine or out at thirty.
Like **running** just to stay in the same place.
S2.quote: There's a version of AGI by 2028 where I'm fine and a version where I'm out at thirty, and I can't tell which.
fieldNote: She turns the **robot gap** into a plan: move to the most human-facing work.
Worries more for her **sister in insurance** than herself, then admits she'd lie awake.
Fast timeline pushes a steady adopter to **commit fully** to AI tools.

steps.text: Transfer to the domestic abuse unit within a year
Skip the summer trip and save up to six months
Take the force's full AI tools course, not just tips
Sign petitions demanding a human officer at every call

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years. I'd be thirty-two. Okay, that's more breathing room than the last one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say what I said before, but I'd say it with a plan attached: let's use the five years to write rules for AI in policing, with the public and the unions in the room. I'd want my force to be the one that gets it right, not the one in the news.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think five years is enough for me. By 2031 I'd hope to be in the domestic abuse unit with a few years of cases behind me. That's work where the paperwork goes to the machine but the sitting-with-people stays, at least until 2034, and probably longer. Nobody wants a robot in a refuge, so the domestic abuse unit is where I'd want to be by 2031.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish the domestic abuse course this year and apply to the unit next year. I'd use the AI tools as they come in, the way everyone else does. And I'd stay on the association working group so I'm in the room when they write the rules.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but in a way I can live with. It's like knowing your building's getting new owners. You don't love it, but you can look for a better flat in time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What about money? Would five years change how you save or spend?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit. I'd keep the four months, nudge it up slowly, and I'd hold off on buying a flat until I'm settled in the unit. I wouldn't cancel everything, though. I'm twenty-seven, I'm not going to live like a monk on a maybe.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you blame if it went badly anyway?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The government, for not planning, and the tech firms, for selling it before anyone understood it. I don't blame the machines, they're tools. It's always about who owns them and who decides.

say: Use five years to write **rules for AI** in policing.
Get the **public and unions** in the room for those rules.
think: Five years is **enough for her** to move into the unit.
Victim work keeps its **human side** past 2034, she believes.
Nobody wants **a robot** in a refuge.
do: Finish the **domestic abuse course** this year, apply next year.
Pick up AI tools **as they arrive**, like colleagues.
Stay on the **working group** writing the rules.
feel: **Uneasy** but able to live with it.
Like a building with **new owners**: time to find a better flat.
S3.quote: Nobody wants a robot in a refuge, so the domestic abuse unit is where I'd want to be by 2031.
fieldNote: Five years matches her **existing plan**, which lowers her worry a lot.
Blames **government and tech owners**, never the tools themselves.
Refuses to **over-save** on a maybe; still lives like a 27-year-old.

steps.text: Finish the domestic abuse course and apply to the unit
Start using each AI tool when the force rolls it out
Keep her seat on the association's rules working group

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. I'd be thirty-seven when it arrives. That's a whole career stage away.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is the version where we have no excuse. Ten years is time to train people, fund the human parts of policing and decide in public what machines can and can't do. If we mess that up it's a choice.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think I'd be all right. By 2036 I'd hope to be a detective in the domestic abuse unit, maybe a sergeant. The machine would do the evidence files and the robot might do the scene search after 2039, but somebody still has to earn a victim's trust. I'd be that somebody.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on as I'm planning anyway: course, unit, then maybe sergeant's exam around thirty-two. I'd learn the AI tools as they're rolled out. And I'd keep turning up at the association, because the rules in ten years get written by whoever bothered to show up now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, mostly. More like curious than scared. My job isn't really about the tasks, it's about being trusted.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there any part of that you'd still worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Budgets. If AI makes the force cheaper, a government might pocket the savings instead of putting them into victim care. That's what happened with every efficiency drive I've heard of from older officers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell a new recruit starting in that world?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell a new recruit to learn the machines but to spend their best energy learning people. The paperwork side of this job is going, but the trust side is the job.

say: With ten years, there's **no excuse** for getting it wrong.
Messing it up would be **a choice**, not an accident.
think: By 2036 she'd hope to be a **detective** in the unit.
Machines take files and scene searches; **trust stays human**.
She expects to be the one who **earns victims' trust**.
do: Follow her plan: **course, unit**, then sergeant's exam near thirty-two.
Keep attending the **association** while rules are written.
feel: Sure her value lies in **being trusted**.
S4.quote: My job isn't really about the tasks, it's about being trusted.
fieldNote: Ten years fits her **career path**, so the change looks manageable or even good.
Her one worry is governments **pocketing savings** rather than funding victim care.
Strong sense of **purpose** anchors her calm.

steps.text: Sit the sergeant's exam around age thirty-two
Learn each new AI tool as the force rolls it out
Attend association meetings on AI rules every quarter

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because it'd land before I'm where I want to be. What would help is the force guaranteeing that any money AI saves goes back into officers and victim services, and paid time for specialist training, not evenings on my own.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about the public. Everyone asks what happens to police jobs, but the bigger question is whether people on the Northgate estate still get a person when they ring. If they don't, it's not just my job that's gone, it's their trust in us.

headlineQuote: The paperwork side of this job is going, but the trust side is the job.
portrait: A **27-year-old neighbourhood officer** who walks a market and housing estate and rents a studio alone.
Values **knowing names** and earning trust; wants to move into the **domestic abuse** unit.
Progressive and union-minded, blaming **budget cuts** and tech owners rather than the tools.
A steady adopter who uses AI **once colleagues prove it**, and commits harder when timelines shorten.
Calm in the slow worlds, **anxious** only when AGI arrives before her specialist move.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, landing before she reaches the domestic abuse unit.
whatWouldHelp: AI savings **reinvested** in officers and victims, plus **paid time** for specialist training.
